  The page calls the actions in actor.ts (list, add, stats), which
  keep rows in SQL: sql/002_shipments.sql made the shipments table
  (sql/001_items.sql is the starter table and is left in place). Each action
  declares the JSON Schema of its arguments and its result; the server checks
  arguments before the action runs. They are the contract: defineAction
  types the action's code from them, and slop types declares the page's
  slop.actions (.slop/types/actions.d.ts).
  Scenarios (scenarios/) run on a fresh test instance, reset and seeded
  from a fixture before each run. add-shipment uses
  fixtures/sample-shipments.json (three shipments from January 2024, so
  only the one it adds through the form counts this week) and checks the
  table, the new row in the data and the week total; stats-match-table
  uses fixtures/week-spread.json (35 rows: 9 this week incl. an 18,000 kg
  oversize, an empty week three weeks back, a 22,000 kg kiln about ten
  months old, one row older than a year, and a 0.1 kg row) and checks every
  number on the This week page against SQL over the same rows, with the
  Monday cutoff recomputed independently in SQL; empty-dashboard checks
  the zero state. The week-spread dates are relative to the week it was
  generated in: when a week rolls over, regenerate them
  (lib.refreshWeekFixture in the bench) and re-run.
  Files are TypeScript; the server compiles them (types are stripped, not
  checked). To check them, pull the app and run slop types <app>: it writes
  the declarations into .slop/types/ and the tsconfig files, then
  tsc -p tsconfig.json checks the pages, and tsc -p tsconfig.actor.json
  the actor.
  Edits in the bench go to the draft ref and your dev instance runs them;
  publishing moves main, which production instances run (their migrations
  run then).
